Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

The delivery notice said the driver would arrive sometime between one and four, and that an adult had to show photo identification because the parcel needed a signature. I moved my afternoon call to the kitchen table and put my keys and wallet beside the blue bowl by the front door so I would not have to look for them later.

At about twelve forty, the tracking page changed to “out for delivery” and showed six stops ahead of ours. I checked that the building entrance was not blocked because a plumber had left a toolbox near the stairs, and I shifted it against the wall. The parcel was addressed to Mara Salcedo at 18 Alder Row, and our buzzer label still said Salcedo even though the landlord had asked us to add my name. I had not done that yet. The notice also showed a note from the sender saying “keep upright,” which mattered because the hinge parts were packed in a narrow cardboard sleeve that could bend if someone pushed it under the door.

My neighbor Joana came out carrying a folded laundry basket while I was checking the notice and asked if I was waiting for the parcel. I said, “Right, that’s the one,” and she offered to keep an eye out from the landing while she sorted her laundry. She is usually home during lunch and can hear the downstairs bell from her flat. She said, “Beleza, I can listen, but I have to take a call at one thirty.” I thanked her and said that was plenty because the tracking estimate had not narrowed yet. Joana put the basket beside her door and left the hall clear so the courier could turn around with a trolley.

The driver rang the bell shortly after two and asked through the intercom, “Are you the person at number eighteen?” I said, “Yes, this is Mara’s brother Daniel, and I can show my identification.” He said, “The label has Salcedo, but the name on the buzzer is hard to read, so I will check it at the door.” I brought my wallet and opened the main entrance but kept the apartment door on its chain while I looked through the side window. His jacket had the parcel company logo, and he held a handheld scanner. He said in German, “Er kommt um halb drei,” when he looked at his route screen. Then he switched back to English and explained that the next scheduled stop was at half past two. I asked whether he meant our parcel or the next one, and he pointed to our address on the screen, so I understood he meant ours.

1. I showed him my photo card, and he compared the street number and surname with the label, then asked me to say the recipient’s full name. I said Mara Salcedo and spelled Salcedo slowly.
2. He looked at the sleeve and asked whether it was fragile. I said the sender’s note says “keep upright” and showed him the side where the instruction was printed.
3. He scanned the parcel, but the first scan did not register, and he tried again after turning the screen toward the window.
4. I signed with my usual short signature and checked that the screen displayed Daniel Salcedo rather than Mara because I was the person accepting it. He handed me the parcel and said, “Please do not leave it in the hallway because the building entrance is shared.”

Before he left, I asked what would happen if I had not been at home. He said, “If nobody answered, I would take the parcel back to the van and leave a card with a collection point and a new pickup window.” He added that the sender had selected “signature required,” so he could not put it behind the recycling bins even if I gave permission over the phone. I asked if Joana could sign for it on another day, and he said only if the delivery account allowed an alternate recipient and the name was entered before the next attempt. I said, “Okay, that makes sense,” and he confirmed that this parcel had now been signed for in person, not left with a neighbor.

Once he had gone, I carried the box inside and set it upright on the kitchen floor rather than on the counter because the screws were loose inside the sleeve. Mara messaged me asking whether it had arrived, and I replied, “Yes, the parcel is here, and I signed for it.” She asked whether the package looked crushed. I checked both ends and told her the cardboard was slightly creased near one corner, but the paper seal was unbroken. Joana called from the landing to ask if the driver had needed help with the trolley. I said no, but thanked her for listening for the bell. She laughed and said she had finished her call just before he arrived.

Mara got home at six and compared the label with the order on her phone. The hinges were the correct size, and all eight screws were in the little bag inside the sleeve. She said the crease did not look serious but asked me to keep the packaging until she had tried one hinge on the pantry door. I left the sleeve upright beside the cupboard and put the signed delivery slip on the blue bowl with my keys. The tracking page later showed “delivered to Daniel Salcedo at 2:07 p.m.,” and its note said “signature captured.” The parcel was in our apartment, and the door still needed its old hinge until Mara had time to test the replacement."}]
